question: A 7-day-old term neonate is having frank convulsions. Blood glucose is 65 mg/dL. Serum total calcium is 5.8 mg/dL (ionised 0.78 mmol/L). You decide to treat with IV calcium gluconate. Which of the following statements about the administration of IV calcium gluconate in neonates is CORRECT?

answers.text: Give 1 mL/kg of 10% calcium gluconate as a rapid IV push over 2–3 minutes to abort the seizure quickly

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect — this is the most dangerous error in neonatal calcium management. RAPID IV calcium causes severe bradycardia, heart block, and cardiac arrest. Calcium gluconate must NEVER be given as a rapid push or IV bolus. It must always be diluted and infused slowly over at least 10–15 minutes with continuous cardiac monitoring.

answers.text: Give 1–2 mL/kg of 10% calcium gluconate diluted in equal volume of 5% dextrose, infused slowly over 10–15 minutes with continuous ECG monitoring

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! IV calcium gluconate in neonates must be given slowly — 1–2 mL/kg of 10% calcium gluconate diluted in an equal volume of dextrose, infused over at LEAST 10–15 minutes under continuous cardiac monitoring (watch for bradycardia — slow or stop if HR drops). Rapid administration causes potentially fatal bradycardia. Extravasation causes severe tissue necrosis — always verify IV patency first.

answers.text: Give calcium chloride 10% at 0.2 mL/kg IV; it is preferred over calcium gluconate in neonates due to better bioavailability

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Calcium chloride is MORE irritant and caustic than calcium gluconate — it causes severe tissue necrosis on extravasation and is generally avoided in neonates for peripheral IV use. Calcium gluconate is the preferred IV formulation in neonates. Calcium chloride may be used in central-line settings by experienced practitioners in refractory cases.

answers.text: Oral calcium supplementation is the first-line treatment for symptomatic neonatal hypocalcaemia with seizures

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Oral calcium is used for MAINTENANCE treatment and for asymptomatic or mild hypocalcaemia. A seizing neonate with severe hypocalcaemia requires immediate IV calcium gluconate (given slowly, as above) to rapidly correct the ionised calcium level and abort the seizure. Oral calcium cannot achieve this rapid correction.

overallFeedback.feedback: KEY RULE for IV calcium in neonates: NEVER give as a rapid push. Always dilute 10% calcium gluconate 1:1 with dextrose and infuse over at least 10–15 minutes under continuous cardiac monitoring. Bradycardia → slow/stop infusion. Symptomatic hypocalcaemia = IV route. Asymptomatic/mild = oral calcium.

The critical rule: IV calcium gluconate in neonates = SLOW infusion (10–15 minutes) + dilution + continuous cardiac monitoring. Rapid push = bradycardia/cardiac arrest. Extravasation = severe tissue necrosis. This is one of the most dangerous errors in neonatal medicine.
